## Learning objectives {#ch12-01 .balanced .stepwise}

- Reconcile and profile each audit population.
- Trace documents and postings in both directions.
- Test purchase matching, approvals, and payroll evidence.
- Retain exceptions, dispositions, and support for conclusions.

::: {.notes}
Purpose: frame SQL as an evidence procedure rather than an exception counter. Allow 60 seconds. The controller has an explanation of recorded manufacturing cost. The audit committee now needs support for the records behind it. Testing every extracted row does not remove extraction risk or establish that transactions occurred as recorded. Ask what evidence would distinguish a flagged record from a supported finding. Transition: specify each test before running it.
:::

# Define and reconcile the population {#ch12-module-2}

::: {.notes}
A reproducible query needs a stated risk, population, criterion, and expected result.
:::

## The committee needs support for the explanation {#ch12-03 .balanced .stepwise}

Does the ledger represent the relevant documents?

Did purchasing controls operate?

Do the time and payroll records support the hours?

::: {.notes}
Purpose: connect the audit procedures with the manufacturing story. Allow 60 seconds. The previous chapter established patterns in recorded costs and hours, not their validity. Each question needs different records and expectations. A coherent ledger can still contain a timing error or an unsupported payment. Ask students to name a source independent of the ledger for each question. Transition: document the test contract.
:::

## State the test before executing SQL {#ch12-04 .balanced .stepwise}

Risk and accounting assertion.

Population, dates, keys, and expected result.

Exception rule, tolerance, and required follow-up.

::: {.notes}
Purpose: make the procedure reviewable. Allow 60-90 seconds. A result should be assessed against an expectation chosen before seeing the exceptions. Some tests expect zero rows; others compare control totals or describe concentrations. A threshold should reflect the procedure's purpose, not be adjusted simply to make a result disappear. Ask students what belongs in the two-line comment above a library query. Transition: reconcile the source population.
:::

## Journal entries reconcile to their ledger postings {#ch12-05 .balanced}

{{< include /_shared/generated/chapter-12/_journal-control.qmd >}}

::: {.notes}
Purpose: demonstrate a count-and-amount control. Allow 60 seconds. The entry table's count and total agree with the related source-document count and ledger debits. Counting distinct source IDs avoids treating every journal line as a different journal. This reconciliation supports the extraction but does not test account classification, authorization, or omitted activity shared by both records. Ask what a balanced but unsupported journal would do to this control. Transition: repeat the principle for manufacturing payroll.
:::

## Manufacturing payroll reconciles by year {#ch12-06 .balanced}

{{< include /_shared/generated/chapter-12/_payroll-control.qmd >}}

::: {.notes}
Purpose: connect the operational cost population with account postings. Allow 60-90 seconds. Register cost includes gross pay plus employer payroll taxes and benefits for the manufacturing cost center. The ledger query independently groups the corresponding PayrollSummary debits. Retain the same cost-center and period definitions on both sides of the comparison. Ask why comparing all-company payroll with manufacturing-only postings would be invalid. Transition: distinguish agreement from completeness.
:::

## Agreement is evidence with a boundary {#ch12-07 .balanced .stepwise}

Two sources can agree and omit the same activity.

Profile dates, statuses, required fields, and keys.

Document what the reconciliation does and does not establish.

::: {.notes}
Purpose: avoid overstating a passed control. Allow 60 seconds. Reconciliation is necessary evidence for the analysis, but common upstream omissions can affect both compared sources. Profiles and independent event records help address that limitation. The procedures that follow examine traceability, cutoff, approvals, and time records. Ask which external or upstream evidence would reveal a missing liability. Transition: trace in both directions.
:::

# Trace documents and test cutoff {#ch12-module-8}

::: {.notes}
Existence, completeness, and timing require different directions and dates.
:::

## Traceability has two directions {#ch12-09 .balanced .stepwise}

**Posting to document:** a recorded event has source support.

**Document to posting:** an eligible source event reached the ledger.

Use source-document type together with its ID.

::: {.notes}
Purpose: connect anti-joins with audit assertions. Allow 60-90 seconds. A missing source record from a ledger trace and an unposted document are different exceptions. The relevant population also needs a status and timing policy: an unapproved draft may not belong in the posting expectation. Type and ID prevent numeric-key collisions across document tables. Ask students which direction they would use for an unrecorded invoice. Transition: read the first anti-join branch.
:::

## An anti-join finds postings without a payment {#ch12-10 .balanced .sql-example}

{{< include /_shared/generated/chapter-12/_query-trace.qmd >}}

::: {.notes}
Purpose: read the payroll-payment branch of the combined trace query. Allow 90 seconds. GLEntry is the left population, and PayrollPayment supplies the supporting record. The WHERE condition selects the source type and tests an absent payment key. This is the first branch of the public query; UNION ALL appends the other document tests. Ask why moving the source-type condition to an unrelated table would change the meaning. Transition: read the returned posting IDs.
:::

## The trace returns six unsupported payment postings {#ch12-11 .balanced}

{{< include /_shared/generated/chapter-12/_trace.qmd >}}

::: {.notes}
Purpose: inspect the public exception list without double counting economic events. Allow 90 seconds. These six rows are ledger postings, not six independent cash payments. The paired postings relate to three approved registers without payment records in the next public test. Retain posting IDs, dates, and the source path for follow-up. Their displayed debit-plus-credit amounts should not be added as though each row were a separate loss. Ask what evidence is needed to determine the payment recipient and authorization. Transition: combine tests while preserving their labels.
:::

## UNION ALL preserves the exception rows {#ch12-12 .balanced .stepwise}

Align columns by position and compatible meaning.

Include a test label and stable record identifier.

Distinguish exception rows from distinct affected documents.

::: {.notes}
Purpose: keep a combined exception library interpretable. Allow 60 seconds. UNION ALL retains duplicates, while UNION removes duplicate result rows. Neither operation determines whether repeated rows represent separate economic events. A document can fail multiple tests, so summing test counts may overstate the number of affected documents. Ask why the trace output includes Test in addition to RecordID. Transition: compare accounting timing with the source event.
:::

## Revenue cutoff compares posting with delivery {#ch12-13 .balanced .stepwise}

Identify the relevant shipment and delivery dates.

Compare the posting year with the delivery year.

Keep unbilled shipments in a separate completeness test.

::: {.notes}
Purpose: examine the event underlying the posting date. Allow 90 seconds. Charles River's tutorial compares the recorded revenue with delivery timing under the case's accounting premise. Invoices with several lines first need their shipment dates summarized at invoice grain. The query separates revenue posted in another year from invoices dated before shipment. Ask why an invoice-date filter alone could miss a delivered but unbilled shipment. Transition: retain the unbilled population.
:::

## Unbilled shipments still require an accounting decision {#ch12-14 .balanced .stepwise}

A left join from ShipmentLine preserves shipped lines.

A missing SalesInvoiceLine identifies an unbilled line.

Inspect delivery, cost posting, and expected billing.

::: {.notes}
Purpose: distinguish the exception criterion from its accounting conclusion. Allow 60-90 seconds. The public tutorial finds December shipments without invoices at the dataset end. Shipment cost and revenue can then fall into different periods. Not every unbilled shipment necessarily satisfies revenue-recognition conditions; the source documents and case assumptions matter. The assigned exercise measures the adjustments, which are not supplied here. Ask what evidence would support inclusion in the year-end revenue population. Transition: apply cutoff reasoning to payroll.
:::

## Payroll pay date is not the work period {#ch12-15 .balanced .stepwise}

Find pay periods that cross year-end.

Identify work earned but not yet processed or paid.

Inspect account 2030 for the related accrual.

::: {.notes}
Purpose: explain why a reconciled paid-payroll population can still miss a year-end liability. Allow 90 seconds. The public records post payroll by pay date. The final periods can therefore contain December work whose cost is not yet in the ledger. An opening balance in Accrued Payroll is not evidence that each subsequent year-end was accrued. Ask students which period fields establish the work and payment dates. Transition: record cutoff findings without unsupported precision.
:::

## Tutorial 12.1: separate reconciliation from cutoff {#ch12-16 .balanced .stepwise}

Retain the count-and-amount controls.

Trace the payment exceptions to their registers.

Document revenue and payroll timing issues separately.

[Open Tutorial 12.1](https://aa.accountinganalyticshub.com/chapters/12-sql-audit-analytics/chapter.html#guided-tutorial-12.1-reconciling-the-populations-tracing-the-ledger-and-testing-cutoff)

::: {.notes}
Purpose: complete the first audit workpaper. Allow three minutes. Students should explain why the ledger reconciles yet year-end timing can be wrong. The tutorial supplies the trace and qualitative cutoff findings; the exercises require separate measurement and conclusions. Ask each pair to state one passed control, one exception, and one remaining evidence request. Transition: test the purchasing chain.
:::

# Match quantities, prices, and approvals {#ch12-module-17}

::: {.notes}
A coherent transaction chain and an effective approval control are separate claims.
:::

## Three-way matching uses the order-line grain {#ch12-18 .balanced .stepwise}

Order quantity.

Total receipts for that order line.

Total invoice quantity for that order line.

::: {.notes}
Purpose: establish the grain before a multi-table comparison. Allow 60-90 seconds. One purchase-order line can have several receipts and invoice lines. Summarize each detail population first, then left-join the summaries to the order line. Joining the raw details together would multiply combinations and overstate quantities. Ask students to name the unique key expected after each aggregation. Transition: classify differences with ordered rules.
:::

## CASE classifies the quantity comparison {#ch12-19 .balanced .stepwise}

Invoiced above received: investigate.

Received above ordered: investigate.

Otherwise distinguish matched, partial, and pending activity.

::: {.notes}
Purpose: interpret the ordered CASE in the public match query. Allow 60-90 seconds. The first true branch controls the displayed status. Numerical tolerances prevent tiny representation differences from becoming exceptions. A pending receipt or incomplete invoice is not automatically a control failure; it can be a normal open process. Ask what happens if the generic matched branch comes before the exception conditions. Transition: inspect the actual status population.
:::

## The quantity statuses show open activity {#ch12-20 .balanced}

{{< include /_shared/generated/chapter-12/_match.qmd >}}

::: {.notes}
Purpose: read the full order-line status distribution. Allow 60 seconds. The public result has no line classified as invoiced above received or received above ordered. It still includes quantities awaiting receipt or invoicing. These categories direct follow-up and accrual work rather than proving the population has no remaining accounting issue. Ask students which category should contribute to the unbilled-receipt control. Transition: compare prices using a stated tolerance.
:::

## The price conclusion depends on the tolerance {#ch12-21 .balanced}

{{< include /_shared/generated/chapter-12/_price.qmd >}}

::: {.notes}
Purpose: make the sensitivity of an exception rule visible. Allow 60-90 seconds. The tutorial's three-percent rule yields no exception, while a two-percent rule retains many lines. The result does not justify choosing the looser threshold after seeing it; the tolerance needs an independent policy or analytical rationale. Ask how students would document the selected threshold and unexpected price behavior below it. Transition: reconcile the open receipt liability.
:::

## Unbilled receipts agree closely with the ledger {#ch12-22 .balanced}

{{< include /_shared/generated/chapter-12/_grni.qmd >}}

::: {.notes}
Purpose: connect purchasing detail to account 2020. Allow 60 seconds. The table preserves the small difference rather than claiming exact agreement. Quantity and price conventions, line rounding, and population definitions should be examined when assessing the difference. The public tutorial accepts agreement within a dollar for this control. Ask what documentation would make that judgment reviewable. Transition: test whether approval actually operated.
:::

## Approval tests need roles, limits, and dates {#ch12-23 .balanced .stepwise}

Compare creator and approver.

Compare order value with approval authority.

Check the approver's employment date and role.

::: {.notes}
Purpose: define separate approval criteria. Allow 60-90 seconds. Employee appears in multiple roles, so use distinct aliases and the correct keys. A current master-file limit or termination date needs a clear effective-date interpretation. The public tutorial uses the available fields as screening criteria; historical policy and authorization evidence may be needed to resolve a flag. Ask what evidence would establish a valid delegated approval. Transition: read the overlapping exception counts.
:::

## Approval-test counts overlap {#ch12-24 .balanced}

{{< include /_shared/generated/chapter-12/_approvals.qmd >}}

::: {.notes}
Purpose: prevent the counts from being added as distinct orders. Allow 60-90 seconds. The same order can be self-approved and above the approver's limit. The public detail query groups flags by PONumber, producing fourteen distinct flagged orders. Retain the set of tests for each order rather than overwriting one with another. An exception requires a documented disposition and supporting approval evidence. Ask which stable identifier belongs in the workpaper. Transition: examine concentration even where individual tests pass.
:::

## Approval concentration can weaken the process {#ch12-25 .balanced .stepwise}

Group by approver ID, not only job title.

Assess the share handled by each person.

Distinguish a missing control design from an isolated failure.

::: {.notes}
Purpose: broaden review beyond individual flagged records. Allow 60 seconds. The public tutorial finds that one person approved almost all purchase orders. That concentration can create capacity and continuity concerns even if many individual approvals satisfy the rule. It does not by itself establish that the approver failed to review any particular order. Ask what evidence would show the depth and timeliness of review. Transition: complete the purchasing workpaper.
:::

## Tutorial 12.2: retain separate conclusions {#ch12-26 .balanced .stepwise}

Reconcile the quantity and unbilled-receipt populations.

Explain the price tolerance.

List distinct flagged orders and approval follow-up.

[Open Tutorial 12.2](https://aa.accountinganalyticshub.com/chapters/12-sql-audit-analytics/chapter.html#guided-tutorial-12.2-matching-purchases-and-testing-their-approvals)

::: {.notes}
Purpose: avoid one broad pass or fail statement about purchasing. Allow three minutes. Students should state which matching tests passed and which approval criteria produced exceptions. The control-design observation about concentration belongs alongside, not inside, a transaction exception count. Ask a partner to trace one order through its creator, approver, limit, and disposition. Transition: test the cost records behind the manufacturing hours.
:::

# Corroborate the records behind the hours {#ch12-module-27}

::: {.notes}
A consistent sequence of recorded hours is valuable evidence, but it is not independent proof of work performed.
:::

## The labor evidence follows several records {#ch12-28 .balanced .stepwise}

TimeClockEntry records attendance.

LaborTimeEntry assigns work and labor type.

PayrollRegisterLine calculates earnings.

Payment and ledger records show settlement and posting.

::: {.notes}
Purpose: map the evidence chain without equating the records. Allow 90 seconds. Each step has a different grain and business meaning. Time may be clocked yet charged to the wrong operation, and a correctly calculated earning may relate to an ineligible person. Counts and hours must be compared at compatible employee and period levels. Ask which link is most independent of the employee-entered operation assignment. Transition: profile the clock population.
:::

## The clock profile exposes scope and missingness {#ch12-29 .balanced}

{{< include /_shared/generated/chapter-12/_time-profile.qmd >}}

::: {.notes}
Purpose: establish what the time extract contains before testing it. Allow 60 seconds. NotApproved and NoClockOut are separate flags and may overlap. The last work date again constrains comparisons with output and operations. Do not calculate an apparently precise duration from an absent clock-out without a stated rule. Ask students which records they would inspect before building a full-period total. Transition: reconcile the chain at compatible grain.
:::

## Clocked, recorded, and paid hours can agree {#ch12-30 .balanced .stepwise}

Compare the three sources by employee and pay period.

Inspect missing links and mismatched employee IDs.

Retain unsupported or unapproved source records.

::: {.notes}
Purpose: make reconciliation more discriminating than a grand-total comparison. Allow 90 seconds. The public tutorial finds that totals agree, while detailed tests identify earnings assigned to other employees and lines resting on unapproved clock entries. Agreement does not clear those exceptions. Testing the low-indirect-time months supports their recorded completeness, but additional operational evidence explains what the plant was doing. Ask why offsetting employee errors could disappear from an all-plant total. Transition: build an independent pay expectation.
:::

## A pay expectation tests the calculation {#ch12-31 .balanced .stepwise}

Hours, employee rate, and overtime rule define expected pay.

Compare each earnings line with its expectation.

Apply the stated line-level threshold before aggregating.

::: {.notes}
Purpose: explain a substantive analytical comparison. Allow 60-90 seconds. The expected amount must use the employee whose work the line represents and the applicable pay rule. A close match supports the arithmetic, not whether the person worked or was authorized. Rate timing and rounding conventions also affect the comparison. Ask which evidence supplies an independent rate and how historical changes would be handled. Transition: distinguish line tolerances from total differences.
:::

## Small line differences can accumulate {#ch12-32 .balanced}

{{< include /_shared/generated/chapter-12/_pay-expectation.qmd >}}

::: {.notes}
Purpose: interpret the result at the tested grain. Allow 60-90 seconds. The public calculation finds no line above its one-cent threshold, while the many small line differences sum to several dollars by year. A nonzero aggregate does not contradict the line-level result. Conversely, a small aggregate could hide offsetting large line errors. Ask students which query result supports the actual exception criterion. Transition: examine overtime authorization and patterns.
:::

## Overtime approval and occurrence are different tests {#ch12-33 .balanced .stepwise}

Check length, approval status, and linked approval records.

Look for identical patterns across many employees.

Corroborate attendance with operational evidence.

::: {.notes}
Purpose: move beyond a checked approval field. Allow 60-90 seconds. The public tutorial finds mostly approved long overtime and a small set with approval-link issues. A shared approver or repeated clock pattern can still need evidence about what work occurred. Do not infer falsification solely from identical times. Ask which production, access, supervisor, or job records would strengthen the explanation. Transition: inspect the surge-day pattern.
:::

## Surge days account for a growing overtime share {#ch12-34 .balanced}

{{< include /_shared/generated/chapter-12/_surge.qmd >}}

::: {.notes}
Purpose: present the public pattern with a defined population. Allow 90 seconds. The tutorial identifies days when all hourly manufacturing employees clock the same hours. The overtime share uses the plant's overtime hours as its denominator. The repeated employee count is part of the pattern, not a claim that every employee in the company worked those days. Ask how the rule should treat absences, staffing changes, or legitimate scheduled shifts. Transition: test which operations received the time.
:::

## Much direct time is charged after the operation ended {#ch12-35 .balanced}

{{< include /_shared/generated/chapter-12/_late.qmd >}}

::: {.notes}
Purpose: connect date logic with the work-center anomaly. Allow 90 seconds. The query joins direct time to its operation and compares WorkDate with ActualEndDate. Its denominator is direct hours in the matched-operation population, which differs from all recorded direct hours. The rising share limits the ability to explain where work occurred from operation assignments alone. Ask which late charge could be legitimate and what evidence would document it. Transition: state the audit implication proportionately.
:::

## Recorded cost needs corroborating evidence {#ch12-36 .balanced .stepwise}

The hours reconcile and pay follows the recorded rates.

Late operation charges weaken the assignment evidence.

Surge-day overtime needs corroboration before reliance.

::: {.notes}
Purpose: synthesize the public tutorial without overstating its evidence. Allow 60-90 seconds. The chain supports that costs were recorded and paid through the system. It does not independently establish the necessity, occurrence, or correct operation assignment of every hour. The accounting and control conclusions should identify exceptions for correction and evidence still needed. Ask students to rewrite a statement that calls every surge-day hour fraudulent into a supportable evidence request. Transition: connect earlier audit techniques to SQL.
:::

## Earlier audit tests translate into SQL patterns {#ch12-37 .balanced .step-rows}

| Audit procedure | SQL pattern |
|---|---|
| Aging and strata | CASE and grouped totals |
| Duplicate keys | GROUP BY with HAVING |
| Sequence gaps | LAG and an ordered key |
| First-digit screening | Expressions and frequencies |

::: {.notes}
Purpose: connect Chapter 8's ideas with the query toolbox. Allow 60-90 seconds. The method changes while the population and interpretation requirements remain. Sequence gaps can reflect valid voids, repeated values can be legitimate, and digit nonconformity is a reason to investigate rather than a fraud conclusion. Ask students to specify a risk and expected result for one translated procedure. Transition: package a repeatable audit library.
:::

## A query library includes dispositions {#ch12-38 .balanced .stepwise}

Save **Audit.sql** with labeled, commented tests.

Retain source versions, parameters, controls, and result IDs.

Record evidence, reviewer, and unresolved follow-up.

::: {.notes}
Purpose: make repeated execution useful for an engagement. Allow 60 seconds. A library needs ownership and a review process when schemas, business rules, or populations change. Rerunning the same SQL is not enough if the assertion or threshold has changed. Store dispositions by stable IDs, not by screen row position. Ask what a reviewer needs to distinguish a carried-forward exception from a new one. Transition: complete the final tutorial.
:::

## Tutorial 12.3 and the audit conclusion {#ch12-39 .balanced .stepwise}

Reconcile the labor chain and review its exceptions.

Explain the pay tolerance and surge-day population.

Separate supported findings from open evidence requests.

[Open Tutorial 12.3](https://aa.accountinganalyticshub.com/chapters/12-sql-audit-analytics/chapter.html#guided-tutorial-12.3-testing-the-hours-behind-the-variance)

::: {.notes}
Purpose: complete the public tutorial and hand off to independent practice. Allow three minutes. Students should retain the three-source hours control, employee and approval exceptions, line-level pay test, and operation-date analysis. The conclusion must distinguish what the records establish from what still needs corroboration. The assigned exercises and Part III case require their own analysis and deliverables; their solutions are not included. Transition: references and attribution.
:::
